articles.text: J. H. Bruem of Taylor, Stark county has, according to the Mandan Pioneer, shown his dishonesty by trying to buy counterfeit money and then shown that he is a consummate fool by kicking, when he found that he was swindled. It appears that he went to New York to buy the "queer" and the man of whom he bought it, put it in a satchel and in Bruem's presence expressed it to Philadelphia, where Bruem wished to stop off to see Independence Hall; a beautiful illustration of a patriotic criminal. When he claimed his satchel in Philadelphia, he found nothing in it but stones. It is beyond doubt that Bruem intended to pass this money among his freinds and neighbors. Stark county's "3-11-77" should give him about two hours to leave the country.
articles.summary: J. H. Bruem of Taylor, Stark county, was swindled when he tried to buy counterfeit money in New York, according to the Mandan Pioneer.

articles.text: Again has Glendive received a "baptism by fire." This is the fifth fire that has occurred there in the last few months and according to report, was the most destructive of any. It completely swept the only business block remaining and now there are only a half dozen business houses and no hotel building left standing. This last fire especially is a crushing blow to Glendive and it is doubtful if she has recuperative power to recover from it. It seems that every new town must pass through this fiery ordeal, and it is only a matter of time when it strikes Medora. With the wind in the same quarter and as strong as it was yesterday, a fire starting on Main street, anywhere between Mrs. Malloy's hotel and Bob. Roberts' saloon, would make a clean sweep of the whole block. It might also jump to Fitzgerald's hotel and from there, burn clear to the Catholic church. This would be a catastrophy which, although not probable, is possible on any day such as yesterday.
articles.summary: A fifth fire destroyed Glendive's remaining business block; the paper warns Medora's Main street is equally exposed.

articles.text: Saturday, the twenty-fourth day of April, has been named by the Governor as Arbor day. This holiday has hitherto been "more honored in the breach than the observance" throughout the Territory; a state of things we hope no longer to see. Although we, in the Bad Lands, are fairly well supplied with trees, there is no one thing that Dakota stands more in need of. In Medora, there are no shade trees except those that grew naturally and there is abundant room for improvement in this respect. There need be little or no expense incurred in planting the trees, as each can dig his own. To help along the movement, if those interested in planting trees will dig them within a reasonable distance of Medora and guarantee to care well for them after being transplanted, we will bring them into town, free of charge. As this will reduce the cash outlay to nothing, we hope to see our offer generally accepted. It will improve the appearance of our town more than any other one thing.
articles.summary: The Governor has named April 24 Arbor day; the Cow Boy offers to haul trees into Medora free for planters.

articles.text: Theodore Roosevelt arrived last Thursday evening and Friday morning started down the river to the Elkhorn ranch. He will remain in the Bad Lands the greater part of the summer. In reference to national politics, he is as outspoken as ever and has effectually cleared himself from any charge of mugwumpery. He thinks that Secretary Garland is in a bad mess through his connection with the Pan-Electric business, as the unadorned fact is that Garland received an immense amount of the stock for no other valuable consideration than that of his influence as a senator and prospective attorney-general, when the only thing that would give value to the stock was a decision of the United States, through the latter office, in its favor. Mr. Roosevelt regards Conkling's re-entry into New York politics as probable, but is by no means in love with that statesman's despotic rule as a leader. Politically, he divides all men into slaves and enemies and the "By Godfrey, I'll never be a slave," was snapped out with a determination that showed there will be strong opposition to Conkling again being the autocrat of the New York Republicans. Mr. Roosevelt is in love with the northwest and were it not for the business and social ties that bind him to New York, would probably reside here permanently.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt arrived in Medora and left for the Elkhorn ranch; the paper reports his views on Garland, the Pan-Electric affair and Conkling.

articles.text: A report was published in the Bismarck Tribune, apparently reliable unless Bro. Quinn happened at the time to be short of copy, of a fight between cowboys and horse thieves about 200 miles above Bismarck on the Big Missouri. Eight cowboys were engaged in a running fight with the thieves and finally brought them to bay on the bank of the Missouri. Here two of them were killed and the other four started across the river on horseback. Two of them broke through and were drowned and the last two surrendered. Coming to shore, they were bound on horses and carried back into the country. If the story is true, there are just six less horse thieves in the west.
articles.summary: Reprinting a Bismarck Tribune report, the paper tells of eight cowboys running down six horse thieves on the Missouri above Bismarck.

articles.text: Green grass has already begun to show, and last Monday we picked several new blades over an inch long. On the old grass, the fresh green was found in numerous instances to extend up two or three inches. This will soon set the cattle to wandering.
articles.summary: New green grass was already an inch or more high on the range.

articles.text: Although the loss in the Bad Lands has been very slight, less than ever before, the average condition of the cattle is probably as poor as it has ever been at this season. There are good fat beeves at present on the range, but they are not as numerous as formerly, while the cows are still further from being in good fix. They will soon begin to pick up rapidly after the second or third week on grass.
articles.summary: Cattle losses were slight but range cattle were in poor condition at winter's end.

articles.text: Owing to the impossibility of gaining perfectly accurate information concerning cattle losses, we have always been reasonably sure of the per cent. of loss in the Bad Lands before publishing the estimate. Even now it is difficult to be exact, but from conservative statements from range riders between the Custer Trail and VI camps, a distance of seventy miles, the whole well-stocked with cattle, the loss cannot exceed two per cent. and it is more likely to run under one per cent. In this district, we have this winter seen thousands of cattle on the range, and have not seen one solitary animal that died during the winter, except two at the Big Plateau bull-camp. This estimate is certainly within bounds and is doubtless a fair one for the whole Bad Lands, as it comes from the most thickly stocked part of them.
articles.summary: The paper estimates winter cattle losses in the Bad Lands at under two per cent, likely under one.

articles.headline: Communication.
articles.text:
Communication.

Bismarck, Dak., March 22, 1886.

A. T. Packard:—

In reply to yours of March 20: The railroad taxes are divided into three parts, two of which remain in the territorial treasrry, and the other is paid to the organized counties theough which the respective lines run, the share of unorganized counties being retained by the territory. The rate per mile, based upon gross earnings has been as follows for that position of the Northern Pacific west of the Missouri rives since its construction there: 1881, $13.18; 1882, $89.92; 1883, $153,70; 1884, $198.88; 1885, $176.65. There is now no provision for the share obtained from that portion in unorganized counties, to be delivered to them upon organization. It would require the enactment of a statute in order that it could be done.

The same state of things exists regarding taxes upon personal property in unorganized counties, assessed amount levied by nearest organized county. The law is found in section 2, chapter 22, laws of 1995, "shall be subject to taxation in the nearest organized county." The way the statue stands now, the relation of an unorganized county to the territory is not that of ward to guardian, but rather of garden to gardener to be cropped without recompense.

If there is anything further which you would like to know in regard to the matter, we would be glad to furnish the information.

Yours to command,
E. W. Caldwell,
Auditor.
articles.summary: Territorial Auditor E. W. Caldwell explains to Packard that unorganized counties such as Billings receive no share of railroad or personal-property taxes collected there.

articles.headline: Estray Law.
articles.text:
Estray Law.

Although we published the estray law Dec. 24, 1885 we find that its provisions are generally misunderstood. The law on the subject is rather complicated but no more so than seems necessary to avoid dishonesty. In this country especially, an animal cannot be considered an estray and subject to being taken up and sold as such unless it is several hundred miles at least from the home ranch. Even then, it is generally a very simple thing to find the owners name by the brand on the animal and no one interested in the cattle business would take up and advertise an animal as an estray unless he was postive that the owner was not in the country. The law takes into consideration the fact, that range animals may wander far from the home ranch and consequently throws every obstacle it can in the way of persons wishing to take an unfair advantage of loose laws on the subject. The very fact the law is so strict and that it is so difficult to obtain ownership of estrays according to law is one of the greatest protections cattlemen have. The following is a synopsis of the full law on the subject.

"Under United States laws, estrays can be taken up only by house-holders and claim-holders and when such estray is found in the immediate vicinity of his or her place of residence in the county where he or she resides, except when the estray is found ten miles from any habitation, in an uninhabited part of the territory.

Estrays cannot be taken up between March 1, and October 1, unless found trespassing.

Whoever takes up an estray, must within fifteen days, give notice of the taking up or finding three times in a weekly newspaper printed in the county where the estray is taken up.

If the estray is not claimed within twenty-two days after the first insertion of the notice, the finder must go before a justice of the peace of the county where he resides and make oath to the facts of the case.

The justice must issue a warrant to three house-holders of the county to appraise the estray, and report a description of the animal and the name and place of residence of the finder to the justice in writing, under oath.

The justice must immediately publish the report and appraisment according to law.

Register of deeds must keep a book entitled 'Estray Register,' and record such reports.

When claim is made for the estray, both the claimant and finder must go before a justice, the claimant make oath to his name, residence and description of property, after all fees and reasonable chargs have been paid the estray must be delivered up.

At the end of one year after the finding if the finder has had the estray advertised and appraised and the appraisment does not exceed fifty dollars, the animal shall belong to the finder.

If the estray is worth more than fifty dollars, notice must be given the justice or his successor who must appoint a day of sale, the sale to be made by the justice at the county seat. The notice must be published three times in a weekly newspaper published in the county. The justice after paying the cost of advertising and all legal costs and charges, pays the residue to the county treasurer and takes his receipt therefor.

If the money is not claimed within six months and proper proof made, the county treasurer shall pay it to the school fund.

The justice must also file with the treasurer a certificate giving a description of the estray, marks and brands and the name of the finder.

The fees of the justice, advertising and appraising must be paid by the finder and be a first lien on the animal.

Any person not authorized, taking up an estray failing to advertise it or imprudently working or failing to feed it properly, shall forfeit to the owner $25 which can be recovered by action for debt before any justice of the peace.

If any estray, after being taken up and advertised, be lost or injured without negligence on the part of the finder, he is not liable to the owner.
articles.summary: The paper explains and summarizes the territorial estray law as it affects range cattle.

articles.text: While we in western Dakota, have been enjoying as beautiful weather as was ever experienced in any country, at any time, Michigan and several other states have been having the worst snowstorms of the season. Except for the high wind of yesterday, the weather for the past four days has been simply perfect.
articles.summary: Fine weather in western Dakota while Michigan and other states had snowstorms; high wind yesterday.

articles.text: Arthur Smith, who declined last week to run for the office of county surveyor, wishes to resign in favor of D. O. Sweet. Mr. Sweet is a practical surveyor, having several years experience at the business and will make a good officer. His name appears to-day in the list of candidates, and we bespeak for him the unanimous vote of the county.
articles.summary: Arthur Smith withdraws for county surveyor in favor of D. O. Sweet, whom the paper endorses.

articles.text: Dr. W. H. Williamson, dentist, from Bismarck, will arrive at Medora on the tenth of April and remain for one week, by request of Howard Eaton. The Dr. is a member of the Dental Examining Board for Dakota and has had many years of experience as a dentist. He will remain only one week.
articles.summary: Bismarck dentist Dr. W. H. Williamson will practice at Medora's Northern Pacific hotel for a week from April 10.

articles.text: We have an over-stock of 3½ Studebaker wagons that the Studebaker M'f'g. Co. have instructed us to close out at $75 each. These wagons have never turned a wheel under a load, are new and first-class in every respect, have the Co's. full guarantee for 5,000 pounds, according to old freighters are the best ironed and easiest running wagon of its size in the world, and cost at the factory, $87 each in car lots. There never has been and never will be again such a bargain in wagons in this country. The $75 rate is cash of course and holds good for one or more. For further particulars, call at or address the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: The Marquis is expected in a few days and immediately on his arrival will prepare for the season's campaign. It is intended to feed as large a number of cattle as possible, as the Co's. retail shops in New York, now open and selling dressed meat from the southern ranges, will after the season commences, draw their supplies from the slaughter-house here. Medora will gain an immense advantage by having the slaughter-house running for eight or ten months in the year as in that event some factories, such as soap, glue and tanning works, could be profitably operated. With the retail markets under the control of the company and no middlemen's profits to pay, we do not see why the feeding plan should fail of success. The principal difficulty encountered last year was in the sale of the dressed beef at profitable rates. The present system of retail markets will do away with this, as meat generally retails for about the same price, no matter what the wholesale price may be.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès is expected soon to start feeding cattle for his company's New York retail shops, supplied from the Medora slaughter-house.

Brand: Bullion Creek Horse Ranch, Jack Bullion, Prop., Medora, Dak. — on left hip; range Bullion creek, twenty miles south of Medora
Brand: N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., Medora, Dak. — also owner of steers purchased of Mason Lovell; ranges Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: Ætna Ranch, Osborne Bros., Proprietors, Medora, Billings Co. — range Knutson creek; horse brand Æ on left hip
Brand: Berry, Boice & Co., Keith, Montana — range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: E. G. Paddock, Medora — circle-dot; ranch four miles north of crossing of N. P. and Little Missouri
Brand: Spring Creek Ranch, L. D. & B. Rumsey; J. L. Truscott, Manager, Medora
Brand: Custer Trail Cattle Co., F. Alden Eaton, Supt., Medora — range Little Missouri river, Deep and Davis creeks
Brand: Neimmela Ranch, Gregor Lang, Manager, P.O. Medora — thistle; range Rough crossing of Little Missouri, Pretty butte
Brand: Bad Lands Cattle Co., M. Wadsworth, Manager, Medora — 7L, bellows, Pd; range Little Missouri river, fifteen miles north of Medora
Brand: Towers & Gudgell, Keith, Montana — OX; range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
articles.summary: Display advertising and cattle and horse brand advertisements on page 4, including Theodore Roosevelt's Chimney Butte Ranch.

events.date_basis: "last Thursday evening" before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Theodore Roosevelt arrives in Medora for the season
events.summary: Theodore Roosevelt arrived in Medora and was expected to remain in the Bad Lands the greater part of the summer.
events.excerpt: Theodore Roosevelt arrived last Thursday evening

events.date_basis: "Friday morning" after last Thursday, before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Theodore Roosevelt goes down the river to the Elkhorn ranch
events.summary: The morning after his arrival, Roosevelt started down the Little Missouri to his Elkhorn ranch.
events.excerpt: Friday morning started down the river to the Elkhorn ranch.

events.date_basis: Interview at his arrival, "last Thursday" before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Roosevelt speaks out on Garland, Pan-Electric and Conkling
events.summary: The paper reported Roosevelt's views that Secretary Garland was compromised by the Pan-Electric stock affair and that he would oppose Conkling's return as autocrat of New York Republicans. It added that he loved the northwest and might live there permanently but for his New York ties.
events.excerpt: "By Godfrey, I'll never be a slave," was snapped out with a determination

events.date_basis: "on the morning of April 13" stated in notice dated issue Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Roosevelt calls Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association meeting
events.summary: Theodore Roosevelt, as chairman, called a meeting of the Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association in the Medora Town Hall at ten o'clock on April 13.
events.excerpt: There will be a meeting of the above association at Medora, on the morning of April 13.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Candidate ticket for first Billings County offices published
events.summary: The paper printed the slate of candidates for Billings County offices, including Dan. McKenzie, J. L. Truscott and John Goodall for commissioner and Fred. A. Willard for sheriff.
events.excerpt: Billings County's Ticket.

events.date_basis: "Second (2nd.) Monday in April, 1886" = 12 Apr 1886
events.title: Billings County organizing election to be held at Medora
events.summary: The Governor's notice called an election at Medora for the first Billings County officers and the temporary county seat, polls open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
events.excerpt: an election will be held for the following officers of said county of Billings

events.date_basis: Polling place for the election on the second Monday in April 1886
events.title: Polls to be in Paddock's livery barn office
events.summary: The judges of election decided to open the polls in Paddock's livery barn office.
events.excerpt: open the polls in Paddock's livery barn office

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: McGinness of Jamestown appointed election supervisor
events.summary: The Governor appointed a Mr. McGinness of Jamestown supervisor of the coming Billings County election.
events.excerpt: The Governor has appointed a Mr. McGinness of Jamestown, to be Supervisor

events.date_basis: "Saturday evening" before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Sheriff Harmon posts election notices in Medora
events.summary: Sheriff Harmon of Morton county came to Medora to post notices for the coming election.
events.excerpt: was here Saturday evening, posting the notices for the coming election.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Arthur Smith withdraws for surveyor in favor of D. O. Sweet
events.summary: Arthur Smith, who had declined to run for county surveyor, asked to resign in favor of D. O. Sweet, whom the paper endorsed.
events.excerpt: wishes to resign in favor of D. O Sweet.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Taylor man swindled buying counterfeit money
events.summary: Citing the Mandan Pioneer, the paper reported that J. H. Bruem of Taylor, Stark county, tried to buy counterfeit money in New York and found only stones in his satchel at Philadelphia.
events.excerpt: he found nothing in it but stones.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Fifth fire wipes out Glendive business block
events.summary: Glendive suffered its fifth and most destructive fire in a few months, leaving half a dozen business houses and no hotel; the paper warned a Main street fire in Medora could sweep the block from Mrs. Malloy's hotel to the Catholic church.
events.excerpt: It completely swept the only business block remaining

events.date_basis: "Saturday, the twenty-fourth day of April" 1886
events.title: Arbor day named; Cow Boy offers to haul trees to Medora
events.summary: The Governor named April 24 Arbor day, and the Cow Boy offered to bring into town, free, trees dug near Medora by people who would plant and care for them.
events.excerpt: we will bring them into town, free of charge.

events.date_basis: Predicted range "between April 5 and 10" 1886
events.title: Missouri River breakup predicted for early April
events.summary: Predictions put the breakup of the Missouri River ice between April 5 and 10.
events.excerpt: Predictions as to when the Big Missouri will break up range between April 5 and 10.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Northern Pacific threatens case against Wells-Fargo
events.summary: The Northern Pacific threatened to reopen its case to keep Wells-Fargo express off the road, though the paper doubted it would reach trial.
events.excerpt: The Northern Pacific railroad threatens to again open up the case against the Wells-Fargo

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Cowboys run down horse thieves on the Missouri
events.summary: Citing the Bismarck Tribune, the paper reported eight cowboys fought six horse thieves 200 miles above Bismarck: two were killed, two drowned and two surrendered.
events.excerpt: If the story is true, there are just six less horse thieves in the west.

events.date_basis: "begins at Miles City, April 19"
events.title: Montana Stockgrowers' spring meeting set for Miles City
events.summary: The Montana Stockgrowers' association spring meeting was to begin at Miles City April 19.
events.excerpt: The spring meeting of the Montana Stockgrowers' association begins at Miles City, April 19.

events.date_basis: "March 31, at two o'clock p. m."
events.title: Round-up No. 7 stockmen to meet at Mingusville
events.summary: A meeting of the stockmen of round-up No. 7 was called at Mingusville for March 31.
events.excerpt: a meeting of the stockmen of round-up No. 7 at Mingusville, March 31

events.date_basis: "last Monday" before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Green grass showing on the range
events.summary: The paper picked new grass blades over an inch long and expected the green to set cattle wandering.
events.excerpt: last Monday we picked several new blades over an inch long.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Bad Lands winter cattle losses put under two per cent
events.summary: From range riders between the Custer Trail and VI camps, the paper estimated winter losses under two per cent and likely under one, though cattle were in poor condition.
events.excerpt: the loss cannot exceed two per cent. and it is more likely to run under one per cent.

events.date_basis: Letter dated "Bismarck, Dak., March 22, 1886"
events.title: Territorial auditor answers Packard on railroad taxes
events.summary: Auditor E. W. Caldwell wrote Packard that the share of railroad and personal-property taxes from unorganized counties stays with the territory and cannot be returned on organization without a new statute.
events.excerpt: not that of ward to guardian, but rather of garden to gardener to be cropped without recompense.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Cow Boy explains the estray law
events.summary: The paper published a synopsis of the estray law, calling its strictness one of cattlemen's greatest protections.
events.excerpt: it is so difficult to obtain ownership of estrays according to law is one of the greatest protections cattlemen have.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday" before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Thermometer reaches seventy-six
events.summary: The thermometer registered seventy-six above.
events.excerpt: Tuesday, the thermometer registered seventy-six above.

events.date_basis: "the past four days" before Thu 25 Mar 1886; high wind "yesterday" = 24 Mar
events.title: Fine spring weather, with high wind on the 24th
events.summary: Western Dakota enjoyed perfect weather for four days, apart from a high wind the day before the issue, while Michigan had snowstorms.
events.excerpt: Except for the high wind of yesterday, the weather for the past four days has been simply perfect.

events.date_basis: "Monday morning" before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Uncle John Seaton returns from the Black Hills
events.summary: Uncle John Seaton came in from the Black Hills and expected to stay all summer.
events.excerpt: Uncle John Seaton came in from the Black Hills, Monday morning.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Germantown visitors at Howard Eaton's ranch
events.summary: Messrs. Thomas and Smith of Germantown, Pa., were visiting Howard Eaton's ranch for a week or two.
events.excerpt: They are now at Howard Eaton's ranch

events.date_basis: "last evening" before Thu 25 Mar 1886; left "this morning" 25 Mar
events.title: F. H. Eaton party arrives from Pittsburgh for the summer
events.summary: Mr. and Mrs. F. H. Eaton, Miss Hattie and Mr. Rook arrived from Pittsburgh and the next morning left for the Logging Camp for the summer.
events.excerpt: arrived from Pittsburgh last evening and this morning started for the Logging Camp

events.date_basis: "the tenth of April" 1886
events.title: Bismarck dentist to practice in Medora
events.summary: Dr. W. H. Williamson, dentist, of Bismarck, was to come to Medora on April 10 for one week at Howard Eaton's request, stopping at the Northern Pacific hotel.
events.excerpt: will arrive at Medora on the tenth of April and remain for one week

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Cow Boy closes out Studebaker wagons at $75
events.summary: The Cow Boy office offered an over-stock of Studebaker wagons at $75 cash on the manufacturer's instructions.
events.excerpt: close out at $75 each.

events.date_basis: "expected in a few days" from Thu 25 Mar 1886
events.title: Marquis de Morès expected; plan to feed cattle for New York shops
events.summary: The Marquis was expected within days to begin feeding as many cattle as possible, with his company's New York retail shops to draw supplies from the Medora slaughter-house.
events.excerpt: The Marquis is expected in a few days and immediately on his arrival will prepare for the season's campaign.
